q: What is a project phase?
options: A collection of logically related project activities that culminates in one or more deliverables or outcomes
The period in which a product is sold in the market
A meeting where the sponsor approves the budget
Any single task assigned to a team member
explanation: A phase groups logically related activities and ends with the completion of one or more deliverables and/or outcomes.

q: At the end of the design phase, senior managers review whether the exit criteria were met and decide whether the project should continue. This review is a:
explanation: A phase gate (stage gate, gate review) checks that outcomes or exit criteria were achieved and leads to a go/no-go decision.

q: Which is a possible decision at a phase gate?
options: Only to continue to the next phase
Only to continue or to request more budget
Only to replace the project manager
To continue, continue with changes, repeat the phase, stay in the phase, pause, or end the project
explanation: Gate decisions include continuing, continuing with modification, ending the project or phase, remaining in the phase, repeating it, or parking the project temporarily.

q: When are risk and uncertainty usually greatest in a project?
explanation: Risk and uncertainty are usually greatest at the start and decrease as decisions are reached and deliverables accepted.

q: How does the cost of making changes typically behave over the life of a project?
options: It is highest at the start and falls over time
It increases as the project progresses
It only matters in adaptive projects
explanation: The cost of changes rises as the project moves toward completion, which is why early stakeholder input is valuable.

q: What is a development approach?
options: The means used to create and evolve the product, service or result during the project life cycle
The phase of the project in which deliverables are built and tested
The organization's hiring policy for developers
The list of features in the product backlog
explanation: The development approach is the method (predictive, adaptive or hybrid). It differs from the development phase, which is a stage where deliverables are created and tested.

q: A project will build a bridge. Requirements are well understood, safety regulations are strict and changes after construction starts are extremely costly. Which approach fits best?
explanation: Clear and stable requirements, rigorous safety and regulatory needs, and costly changes all point to a predictive approach.

q: A startup is creating a new mobile app. Customer needs are unclear and the team expects features to change after each round of user testing. Which approach fits best?
explanation: High uncertainty, changing requirements and the value of frequent feedback point to an adaptive approach.

q: Which terms are other names for the predictive approach?
explanation: Predictive is also called waterfall, plan-driven or traditional. Adaptive is also called change-driven or agile.

q: What is the difference between iterative and incremental development?
options: Iterative refines the work through repeated cycles; incremental delivers small usable pieces that build on each other
Iterative is predictive; incremental is adaptive
Iterative delivers once at the end; incremental never delivers
They mean exactly the same thing
explanation: Iterative focuses on refining and improving through repeated cycles. Incremental delivers the product in small usable segments that each add value.

q: In an adaptive project with fixed timeboxes and a fixed team, an unexpected change appears. Which constraint normally varies to absorb it?
explanation: This is the inverted triangle: when budget and schedule are fixed, unexpected changes are managed by varying scope.

q: A company develops software using short iterations, while the data center that will host it is built from a detailed up-front plan. The overall project is using:
explanation: One deliverable is adaptive and the other predictive, which is the book's own example of a hybrid approach.

q: What does the PMBOK Guide, Eighth Edition, say about hybrid approaches?
options: They should be avoided, because mixing approaches confuses the team and the sponsor
Most projects today can benefit from combining adaptive and predictive elements
They are only for software projects
They are the same as incremental delivery
explanation: The standard states that most projects can strongly benefit from a hybrid approach; relying on only one approach is no longer sufficient for modern complexity.

q: A team limits the number of items being worked on at the same time and visualizes work on a board, aiming for continuous flow. This describes:
explanation: Kanban is a visual workflow management method that limits work in process (WIP), based on lean principles.

q: A software team releases a working update to users every two weeks on a fixed schedule. Which delivery cadence is this?
options: Multiple deliveries with no fixed schedule
explanation: Periodic deliveries are like multiple deliveries but on a regular, fixed schedule. They are common in adaptive approaches.

q: Which organizational factor makes an adaptive approach a more natural fit?
options: A rigid functional hierarchy with strict lines of authority
A culture of directing work and measuring against fixed baselines
Very large teams spread over many layers of management
A culture that embraces uncertainty and self-managed teams
explanation: Adaptive approaches fit cultures that embrace uncertainty, self-managed teams, flexible thinking and innovation, and often work better with smaller teams.

q: Who typically chooses the development approach for a project?
options: The project manager, in consultation with the project management team
The supplier with the largest contract
explanation: The choice is typically made by the project manager in consultation with the project management team, based on the nature of the project.

q: At a phase gate the exit criteria have been met, but a more urgent initiative needs the same team for the next two months. Which gate decision fits?
options: End the project, because the team is not available
Repeat the whole phase, to keep the team busy until the other work is finished
Park the project temporarily for the more urgent initiative
Continue to the next phase with no team assigned
explanation: Possible decisions at a phase gate include continuing, continuing with modifications, ending, remaining in the phase, repeating it, or parking the project temporarily for a more urgent initiative.

q: On a predictive building project, the customer asks to move a staircase. During design the change would have taken a day. Now the walls are up. Why is the same change so much more expensive?
options: Because risk and uncertainty are highest near the end
Because stakeholders have more influence over scope near the end of a project
Because staffing is lowest during the build work
Because the cost of changes rises as the project progresses
explanation: The cost of changes is low at the start and high toward the end, while stakeholders' ability to influence scope cheaply decreases. This is why resolving uncertainty early is cheaper.

q: A new highway is fully designed and planned before work starts. It is then opened to traffic one section at a time, each section adding to the last. Which approach is this?
options: Hybrid with an adaptive rollout at the very end
explanation: In predictive work with incremental delivery, the whole scope is understood and planned up front, but the product is delivered in parts. Stakeholders get value earlier while scope and timeline stay largely fixed.

q: A team's work piles up in front of the single test environment while every other step has spare capacity. The team decides to fix that one limiting step before improving anything else. Which idea is it applying?
explanation: The theory of constraints says to find and fix the single most limiting factor standing in the way of the goal. It is one of the sources of flow-based scheduling, alongside Kanban.

q: A web service is updated many times a week. Each small change is tested automatically and then flows straight into production. Which delivery cadence is this?
explanation: In continuous delivery, tested increments flow to production on an ongoing basis, supported by automation. Periodic deliveries follow a fixed regular schedule, such as every two weeks.

q: A status report says: "The project is now in the stage where the deliverables are built and tested." A stakeholder replies: "So the development approach is build and test?" What should the project manager clarify?
options: That the stakeholder is correct, since the two terms mean the same thing in the Guide
That the approach is chosen by the customer during this stage
That this is the development phase; the approach is how the product is created
That a development approach exists only in adaptive projects
explanation: A development approach is the means used to create and evolve the product: predictive, adaptive or hybrid. The development phase is the stage of a life cycle where deliverables are actually built and tested.

q: A training course is built in three modules by different people. Each module adds to the last, but the course can be used only once all three are finished and joined. In the 7th edition's terms, which approach is this?
options: Iterative, because each module is tried out and improved
Predictive, because all three modules are planned
Continuous delivery, because modules keep arriving
Incremental, because it is complete only after the final iteration
explanation: In the 7th edition an incremental approach produces a deliverable through a series of iterations, each adding functionality; the deliverable is considered complete only after the final iteration. An iterative approach is for clarifying requirements and investigating options.

q: A project's test phase may not begin until the test laboratory has been booked and the test plan approved. What are these two conditions, as attributes of the phase?
explanation: Entrance criteria are what must be true to start a phase. Exit criteria are what must be true to finish it. Both are attributes of a phase, with its name, number, duration and resource requirements.

q: Before the build phase of a project starts, a review confirms that the work still fits the organization's goals, that resources are available and that planning is complete. Where does this gate sit, and what is it called?
options: At the end of the build phase; a closing review
In the middle of the phase; a status meeting
At the start of the phase; a pre-phase gate
After the project closes; a benefits review
explanation: A phase gate usually sits at the end of a phase. Gates can also be placed at the start of a phase, as pre-phase gates, to confirm alignment, resources and planning before work begins.

q: On a predictive project, the approved scope, the approved schedule and the approved cost are managed as one reference against which performance is measured. What does the Eighth Edition call the three together?
explanation: In a predictive approach the scope, schedule and cost baselines together are the integrated baseline. Executing aims at the value that baseline represents.

q: A drug development project hands over results at several points: after each trial phase, at regulatory approval and at launch. The dates depend on the work and follow no fixed rhythm. Which delivery cadence is this?
explanation: Multiple deliveries: components are delivered at different times, in sequence or in parallel. Periodic deliveries are like multiple ones but on a fixed, regular schedule.

q: A project runs almost entirely in two-week iterations with a backlog. One part, a hardware order with a long lead time, is planned and controlled in the traditional way. Which Disciplined Agile level of hybrid is this?
options: Level 3: adaptive dominates, with some predictive elements
It is not hybrid at all, because one approach clearly leads the other
explanation: Disciplined Agile describes three levels of hybrid. Level 1: predictive dominates with some adaptive elements. Level 2: both contribute significantly. Level 3: adaptive dominates with some predictive elements.
